transcript:
Meeting: POC weekly check-in - reliability / throttles / timeouts
Date: 2027-10-12
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Connor Lee (Redwood SE), Olivia Martinez (NimbusPay Eng Mgr), Rajesh Gupta (NimbusPay Backend), Samantha Lee (NimbusPay SRE), Ethan Cole (NimbusPay Product)

Summary:
- Reviewed last week's spike that produced intermittent 502/5xx during peak card tokenization flow.
- Agreed on an immediate staging stress test and a set of retry/backoff config changes.
- Decided to instrument a sliding throttle window and to try graceful degradation (short responses) for the non-critical paths.

Topics:
- Queue depth and in-flight request limits
- Server-side throttle windows and client retry budget
- Timeouts (connect vs request-level) and perceived tail latency
- Fallback design for non-blocking features

00:00 Maya: all right everyone, thanks for jumping on. quick call today, want to go over the spike from last friday and the mitigations we tried, and then the follow-ups. can you everyone hear me?
00:10 Olivia: yep loud and clear. thanks Maya.
00:15 Rajesh: yep hi. sorry we're a little late, had a deploy and the pager went off.
00:20 Maya: totally, no worries. Connor, do you want to kick off with the telemetry?
00:25 Connor: sure. so we pulled the telemetry from the pilot cluster and what we see is two bursts of traffic between 14:30 and 14:40 where queue depth jumped from ~200 to about 1.2k, our per-tenant concurrency cap was hit which caused requests to queue in front end LB and then the backend started iterating retries, leading to amplification and downstream 502s. there was also a KV cache miss storm that increased token generation time slightly.
00:55 Samantha: quick question, when you say concurrency cap — is that the per-worker in the redwood runtime or the request router global limit? i think our infra saw socket backlog grow.
01:03 Connor: good point. it's the runtime per-worker soft cap plus the routing layer that does admission. we saw both the worker queue and router window get saturated. sometimes those names get flipped in the transcripts — e.g., the router called "route-adm" — so it's a bit messy in the logs.
01:18 Rajesh: ok that matches what we saw. we also had a surge of long-running requests from a batch of customers hitting a v1 gateway that does synchronous validations.
01:28 Olivia: yeah the tokenization path is synchronous for PCI check, so tail latency hurts.
01:33 Maya: so two levers we suggested last week: lower per-tenant concurrency (which forces early 429s instead of downstream 502s) and enable short-circuit fallbacks for non-critical flows. also tuning client retry to a smaller retry budget.
01:48 Ethan: can you elaborate on short-circuit fallback? like what would user-visible impact be?
01:53 Connor: sure — for non-blocking enrichments we return minimal fields or cached stubs, so the payment flow can continue, then async backfill. the UX impact is small and it's strictly for non-essential data.
02:07 Samantha: i like that but we need end-to-end audit logs for any async backfill so we can reconcile payments. will that break our compliance?
02:15 Maya: good flag. Redwood's event logs and audit pipeline can be set to stream to your KMS-backed storage; i'll include the security doc link after the call. note: i said K M S in the call but sometimes the transcript shows KMS as K M S — apologies if the auto-text is weird.
02:30 Rajesh: also want to confirm how rate windows work — like if you set a 1-minute window vs a 5-minute sliding window, what are the tradeoffs?
02:38 Connor: shorter window means you surface failures faster but can oscillate if traffic is bursty; longer window smooths bursts but delays backpressure. for this use case i recommend a 30s sliding window for admission, plus a burst token bucket on the router for occasional spikes.
02:55 Olivia: does Redwood Dedicated or Hosted behave differently here? we've been testing on the hosted pilot but are evaluating Dedicated for isolation.
03:03 Maya: behavior is same from an API perspective; Dedicated gives you reserved capacity so the bursts are less likely to coincide with noisy neighbors, but you still need admission and retry logic. we sometimes call the private on-prem option 'Redwood Private' in docs and the transcript may show 'Redwood Privatey' or 'redwood private plane' — ignore those mis-hearings.
03:20 Rajesh: cool. about retries — we currently have client retry set to 3 fast retries with no jitter, which likely contributed to retry amplification.
03:28 Connor: yep remove immediate retries. recommended pattern: 1) client-level exponential backoff with initial 200ms and jitter, max 2 retries for idempotent calls; 2) for tokenization path mark as non-idempotent and prefer fail-fast + fallback.
03:45 Samantha: can you share recommended code snippet? our client SDK is in golang.
03:50 Connor: absolutely, i'll paste the snippet in the slack thread and add a go example in the runbook.
03:55 Maya: we also measured the KV cache hit ratio — during the spike it dropped from 92% to 58% which explains increased tokenization latency.
04:05 Rajesh: why would cache drop? were keys evicted due to memory pressure?
04:09 Connor: it looks like a combination of cold keys from a new campaign plus concurrent cache shards being warmed. we can increase pre-warm and use sticky routing to improve locality.
04:18 Olivia: sticky routing — is that available in hosted right now?
04:22 Connor: yes in the hosted runtime we have session affinity options. we'll share config snippets.
04:29 Ethan: one other ask — can we get a tighter SLO definition for tail latency? currently our SLA is 95th < 150ms but we care about 99.9th for user-visible flows.
04:40 Maya: that's a common ask. Redwood Console can surface 99th/99.9th percentiles per route. for the pilot we can instrument a dashboard and export the window to you.
04:50 Samantha: nice. also we want to understand how Redwood's automatic batching interacts with our per-request timeouts. sometimes batching extends the single-request latency.
04:59 Connor: batching optimization is workload-aware — it will not hold a request longer than your rpc timeout threshold. however small timeouts plus batching can cause more timeouts if the batch waits. we recommend setting a slightly larger request timeout for batched routes or use a fast-path route that disables batching for latency-sensitive endpoints.
05:20 Rajesh: ok that helps. let's go over the concrete plan — what are the changes this week?
05:25 Maya: proposed plan: 1) Rajesh to share production peak qps histograms and 5xx traces; 2) Connor to run 2-hour stress in staging on 10/15 simulating your peak mixes; 3) Maya to send tuned runbook (retry/backoff, per-tenant concurrency, throttle window settings, fallbacks) and benchmark spreadsheet by 10/14; 4) Customer to try client retry changes in a small canary and report.
05:47 Olivia: timeline sounds good. curious on the stress test setup — will it mimic sticky sessions and client behavior?
05:53 Connor: yes we'll replay real traffic shape including session affinity, hot keys, and the worst-case long requests. we'll produce a runbook and attach logs.
06:02 Samantha: on the logs — can Redwood redact pci fields automatically? we need to avoid card data in logs.
06:09 Maya: absolutely — the platform supports PII redaction and you can route logs to your own S3 with KMS encryption. i'll include the compliance summary in the email.
06:20 Rajesh: slight tangent — our security team asked about SAML SSO for console access and RBAC separation for dev vs prod access. where do we stand?
06:29 Maya: Redwood supports SSO via SAML/OIDC and fine-grained RBAC. we'll share the enterprise onboarding doc — there was a version mismatch in a previous pdf where "RBAC" became "R-B AC" in the transcript, so ignore that.
06:41 Olivia: thanks. any concerns about the cost delta if we raise reserved capacity or enable more warm pools? budget is a constraint.
06:48 Maya: yes cost is a tradeoff. in the spreadsheet i'll include conservative estimates for dedicated capacity vs warm pool sizing and optimistic optimized quantization suggestions. note: quantization here refers to model runtime optimizations and shouldn't be confused with your data quantization — apologies if that came across funky in the auto text.
07:06 Ethan: earlier you mentioned graceful degradation returning short responses. do you have a sample schema for that?
07:11 Connor: yes we'll attach a small example: for enrichment fields we return a minimal object with a "degraded": true flag and a link to later fetch full data. that'll be in the runbook.
07:20 Rajesh: ok i want explicit action item — we need a failover matrix showing when to route to a smaller, faster model vs queue and when to return 429s.
07:28 Maya: we can produce that. i'll add it to the runbook and send a one-pager.
07:33 Samantha: what about circuit breaker thresholds? our system uses an adaptive circuit breaker today. how do these interact?
07:40 Connor: Redwood's routing respects client circuit breakers; however we recommend a coordinated window: 1) client-side CB for endpoint-level failures; 2) server-side admission with token bucket; 3) an optional global CB for system-level degradations. we'll document how to tune thresholds so you don't get into thrash.
07:58 Olivia: i want to make sure the follow-up includes the raw 5xx traces — sometimes stack frames in the trace are obfuscated in the hosted logs.
08:05 Connor: we'll provide full traces with obfuscation options turned off for your SREs and scrub sensitive fields.
08:12 Rajesh: perfect. last technical quick question: what's the recommended connect timeout vs request timeout for your runtime? we currently use connect=50ms and request=350ms.
08:21 Connor: connect 50ms is aggressive; i suggest connect 100ms, request 800ms for tokenization flow if you are enabling batching; for the super low-latency path keep request 300ms and disable batching.
08:34 Samantha: noted. we'll try those values in the canary.
08:39 Maya: ok let's recap next steps. (recap) Connor will run the 2-hour stress on 10/15 and attach logs; Rajesh to send peak qps and traces by 10/13; Maya to send runbook and cost delta by 10/14; Samantha to test client backoff and report by 10/16; schedule follow-up for week of 10/18.
09:03 Olivia: are we good to close? any blockers?
09:06 Rajesh: none on our side.
09:08 Ethan: none here.
09:09 Maya: great, thanks everyone. i'll follow up with links: runbook, security pdf, benchmark sheet and put Connor's stress plan in the thread.
09:18 Connor: thanks all. bye.
09:20 Meeting ended.
